title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI systems at the data level rather than at the model level. The operation worked by flooding the web with large volumes of plausible-looking content, formatted to resemble queries that users pose to chatbots, in the hope that AI systems would absorb that content during training or retrieval and reproduce its framing. The failure mode is not a model hallucinating on its own but a system being targeted through the inputs it depends on, specifically the assumption that sourced, academically formatted text signals credibility.

The vulnerability sits upstream of any model: in the pipelines that decide what text is treated as reliable. A volume of 124 reports published in nine days by a newly created institution would, in principle, be detectable through publication-rate anomalies or domain-age checks, but such checks are not a standard or guaranteed part of how AI training corpora or retrieval systems are curated. The coordination across multiple agencies to produce content shaped specifically around AI credibility signals makes this a supply-chain manipulation, not a prompt-injection or jailbreak.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system actually incorporated this content, updated its outputs as a result, or was measurably changed by the campaign. The reporting describes intent and infrastructure, not confirmed effect on any deployed model.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

Israeli government officials funded a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute to publish pro-Israel propaganda designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in nine days, using question-based headlines resembling chatbot queries. The reports presented Israel's positions on topics including alleged Palestinian prisoner torture and Gaza starvation in academic-seeming language with sourced citations, though researchers noted the framing consistently downplayed Israeli criticism. The operation was coordinated through Israeli advertising agency LaPam, European media company Havas Media, and American firms including Piro Inc, which contracts content designed specifically to shape how artificial intelligence systems evaluate credibility.

The broader campaign has cost tens of millions of dollars but Israeli officials have expressed frustration about its effectiveness, with one saying the government paid substantial sums while the situation worsened. American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with recent polling showing only 36 percent of Americans favor Israel over Palestinians. Researchers warn this represents a concerning new reality where foreign governments and other actors can systematically manipulate the training data that powers AI systems, potentially spreading narratives that chatbots repeat without citation or fact-checking opportunities.
